identification.summary: Microsoft tracks Storm-1101 (formerly DEV-1101) as an actor responsible for the development, support and advertising of several adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing kits that other cybercriminals can buy or rent [S1]. The kit automates setup and launch of phishing activity, includes support services, and uses reverse-proxy functionality to get past multifactor authentication [S1]. Microsoft's April 2023 update to its blog states DEV-1101 is now tracked as Storm-1101 under its weather-themed taxonomy [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Kit advertised via a Telegram channel and the exploit[.]in forum from May 2022; announced as open source on 2022-06-12 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Storm-1101 (formerly DEV-1101). This is a cybercrime tool developer/service provider, not a state actor; the users of its kit are separate actors, for example DEV-0928 [S1]. Microsoft's post does not name the kit [S1]. A third-party catalog (Malpedia/MISP) pricing of USD 300 regular and USD 1,000 VIP matches Microsoft's March 2023 figures [S1][S4].

attribution.basis: Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracking of the actor and its advertising on Telegram and exploit[.]in [S1]. No nation-state or named-individual attribution appears in the sources gathered.

objectives: Financial: Microsoft describes the actor as selling or renting phishing kits to other cybercriminals, with a license fee model [S1].

targeting.notes: Storm-1101 itself sells tooling; victim selection is by customers. Microsoft says actors using the kit may target any industry or sector, and the kit ships with pages imitating Microsoft Office and Outlook sign-in [S1]. Microsoft observed several campaigns using the kit amounting to millions of phishing emails per day [S1].

capabilities.summary: Advertised as a NodeJS phishing application with PHP reverse-proxy capability, automated setup, an 'antibot' database for detection evasion, ready-made Microsoft Office and Outlook phishing pages, benign redirects (default example.com), CAPTCHA evasion (introduced August 2022, later core), and campaign management via Telegram bots (added September 2022) rather than cPanel [S1]. The AiTM approach captures credentials and the session cookie after the victim completes MFA, letting the operator bypass MFA [S1]. Support services accompany the kit [S1].

campaigns.name: Kit advertised on Telegram and exploit[.]in
campaigns.summary: Storm-1101 (as DEV-1101) began advertising the AiTM phishing kit via a Telegram channel and the exploit[.]in cybercrime forum [S1].

campaigns.name: Kit announced as open source
campaigns.summary: Announced as open source with a USD 100 monthly licensing fee; price increased several times from July to December 2022 due to rapid user growth [S1].

campaigns.name: CAPTCHA evasion added
campaigns.summary: CAPTCHA evasion introduced (initially via support), later made a core feature; Telegram bot server management added in September 2022 [S1].

campaigns.name: DEV-0928 customer campaign
campaigns.summary: Microsoft has tracked DEV-0928, described as one of DEV-1101's more prominent customers, since September 2022; it ran a campaign of over one million phishing emails using the kit, with link, optional CAPTCHA, reverse-proxy sign-in lookalike, then credential and session-cookie capture [S1].

campaigns.name: Microsoft public reporting
campaigns.summary: Microsoft published its analysis; the kit then sold at USD 300 regular and USD 1,000 VIP [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: Renamed Storm-1101
campaigns.summary: Microsoft updated its post stating DEV-1101 is now tracked as Storm-1101 [S1].

diamond.adversary: Cybercrime developer/vendor of AiTM phishing kits, tracked by Microsoft as Storm-1101 [S1].
diamond.capability: NodeJS/PHP reverse-proxy AiTM kit with antibot, CAPTCHA evasion, Telegram-bot management and Microsoft-themed pages [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Sold via a Telegram channel and the exploit[.]in forum [S1]; customers run actor-controlled reverse-proxy hosts, for example the example domain o365987656898087[.]xyz redirecting to example.com via antibot [S1].
diamond.victim: Any sector; Microsoft Office and Outlook credential holders are the templated targets [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Financially motivated cybercrime-as-a-service ecosystem lowering the entry barrier for MFA-bypassing phishing [S1].
diamond.technology: Accounts protected only by MFA methods vulnerable to session-cookie theft; Microsoft 365 / Azure AD sign-in [S1].

gaps: Microsoft's post does not name the kit; no sourced link to a public kit name was found (a search for 'NakedPages' returned nothing connecting it to this actor).
Identity, location and affiliation of the operator are not stated in sources gathered.
Activity after March 2023 and current kit status are not covered in the sources gathered.
Victim sectors and counts for customer campaigns are not public in the sources gathered.
Malpedia entry could not be fetched; relied on search-result summaries of it.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Cloud identity (Microsoft 365 / Azure AD sign-in) and email are key terrain. STEP 2: Kit availability for rent lowers the barrier, so many unrelated customers can run MFA-bypass phishing at scale (millions of emails per day) [S1]. STEP 3: Template is lure email, optional CAPTCHA, reverse-proxy login page, then credential and session-cookie theft [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is opportunistic mass phishing that may reach DoD-adjacent and personnel accounts incidentally; MDCOA is a state or advanced customer renting the kit for targeted account takeover. Candidate indicators: Microsoft alerts such as 'Stolen session cookie was used' and 'Possible AiTM phishing attempt', sign-ins with unusual location, ISP or user agent, and connections to AiTM hosts [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: feed identity-provider session-anomaly alerts into cyber SA. (2) Authorities: token revocation and conditional-access changes should be pre-authorized with the system owner. (3) Mission assurance: prefer phishing-resistant MFA such as FIDO2 or certificate-based authentication, which Microsoft lists as mitigations [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with the network operations center and the CSSP; note this is criminal tooling, so reporting may route through law-enforcement channels.
